intro: Inside a battery system, two devices talk all the time: the battery management system (BMS), the battery's own guardian, and the power conversion system (PCS), which charges and discharges it. They often share a CAN bus: one pair of wires, first made for cars, on which every device hears every message. A CAN frame is short: an identifier and up to 8 data bytes, with no sender address. CANopen gives the identifiers a meaning: which node (device on the bus) sends, and what kind of message it is.
plain: Inside a big battery, a small computer watches every cell, and a power converter moves energy in and out. They talk over one shared pair of wires, like people in one room where everyone hears everything. Each message starts with a label that says who sent it and what it is about, so each listener picks out what matters to it. Most readings are sent on a schedule without anyone asking, and alarms go out at once.

boot.title: BMS starts up
boot.text: The BMS, node 5 on the bus, powers up and sends one boot-up message. It is now pre-operational, a waiting state. It answers SDO requests, one-off questions about a single value, but sends no process data, the live readings.

identify.title: Check the identity
identify.text: The PCS is the NMT master (network management): it starts and supervises the other nodes. It reads the BMS's serial number with an SDO. Every value in a CANopen device has an address in its object dictionary, a numbered list: the serial number is object 0x1018, sub-index 4.

start.title: Start the BMS
start.text: The PCS tells node 5 to go operational, its working state. From now on, the BMS sends its process data, and a heartbeat every second: a short "I am alive" message.

data.title: Live readings
data.text: TPDO1 is the BMS's first transmit PDO: a process data object, one message of live values. Every 100 ms it carries the pack voltage, the current, the state of charge (how full the battery is) and the hottest cell's temperature. Nobody asks and nobody answers: the PCS just listens. The BMS maker's EDS file, an electronic data sheet, says what each byte means.

alarm.title: Cell too hot
alarm.text: A cell in module 3 reaches 61 °C. The BMS sends an emergency message (EMCY) at once. The PCS cuts the current to 40 A.

recover.title: All clear
recover.text: The cell cools down. The BMS sends an emergency message with error code 0x0000: the error is gone.

frames.emcy: Emergency: a cell is too hot

id-705.name: Identifier 0x705
id-705.note: 0x700 + node 5: node 5's boot-up and heartbeat. 11 bits on the wire, shown here in 2 bytes.

id-605.name: Identifier 0x605
id-605.note: 0x600 + node 5: an SDO request to node 5. 11 bits on the wire.

id-585.name: Identifier 0x585
id-585.note: 0x580 + node 5: an SDO response from node 5. 11 bits on the wire.

id-000.name: Identifier 0x000
id-000.note: NMT. When two nodes send at once, the lower identifier goes first, so this one wins against every other frame. Only the NMT master sends it.

id-185.name: Identifier 0x185
id-185.note: 0x180 + node 5: TPDO1, the first process data object node 5 sends. 11 bits on the wire.

id-085.name: Identifier 0x085
id-085.note: 0x080 + node 5: node 5's emergency message. Its low identifier gives it priority over PDOs, the process data.

dlc-1.name: DLC 1
dlc-1.note: One data byte. The data length code is 4 bits on the wire, shown here in 1 byte.

dlc-6.name: DLC 6
dlc-6.note: Six data bytes. The BMS's PDO mapping, object 0x1A00, says which value goes in which bytes.

dlc-8.name: DLC 8
dlc-8.note: Eight data bytes: SDO and emergency messages always have 8.

state-boot.name: State 0x00
state-boot.note: Boot-up: node 5 has started and is now pre-operational.

sdo-upload.name: Command 0x40
sdo-upload.note: Initiate upload: send me the value of an object. "Upload" means from the node to the client.

sdo-expedited.name: Command 0x43
sdo-expedited.note: Upload response, expedited: the value is in this frame, and it has 4 bytes.

index-1018.name: Index 0x1018
index-1018.note: Low byte first: object 0x1018, the identity object.

sub-4.name: Sub-index 4
sub-4.note: The serial number. 1 is the vendor ID, 2 the product code, 3 the revision.

reserved.name: Reserved
reserved.note: Four zero bytes: a read request carries no data.

nmt-start.name: Command 0x01
nmt-start.note: Start remote node: go operational. 0x02 stops it, 0x81 resets it.

nmt-node.name: Node 5
nmt-node.note: The node that must start. 0 would start every node on the bus.

volt.name: Pack voltage
volt.note: 0x1FBC = 8124, in steps of 0.1 V: 812.4 V. Low byte first, like all CANopen numbers.

amp.name: Pack current
amp.note: 0x05F3 = 1523, in steps of 0.1 A: 152.3 A. For this BMS, positive means discharging.

amp-low.name: Pack current
amp-low.note: 0x0190 = 400: 40.0 A. The PCS has cut the current.

err-4200.name: Error code 0x4200
err-4200.note: Low byte first: device temperature, in the class of temperature errors (0x4xxx).

errreg-09.name: Error register 0x09
errreg-09.note: A summary of active errors, also kept in object 0x1001: bit 0 (some error) and bit 3 (temperature) are set.

emcy-maker.name: Maker's data
emcy-maker.note: Five bytes the BMS maker defines. This one sends module 3, cell 12 (0x0C) and 61 °C (0x3D).

err-0000.name: Error code 0x0000
err-0000.note: Error reset: no error is active any more.

a-function.name: Function code
a-function.note: The top 4 bits: the kind of message. 0011 = 3: TPDO1, 0x180 in the identifier.

a-node.name: Node ID
a-node.note: The low 7 bits: which node. 0000101 = 5: the BMS. A bus has room for nodes 1 to 127.

facts.between: BMS ↔ power conversion system, inside one battery system
facts.transport: A CAN bus: two wires (CAN_H, CAN_L), 120 Ω at each end
facts.frames: NMT · heartbeat · PDO · SDO · EMCY, each on its own identifier
facts.speed: 500 kbit/s here: a frame with 8 data bytes takes about 0.25 ms

tips: Many battery makers use their own CAN messages, with their own identifiers and scaling, not CANopen. CANopen is one common standard way. Ask for the maker's EDS file or CAN message list before you connect.
Two nodes must never send the same identifier. In CANopen, every node ID on the bus must be unique.
Watch the heartbeat. Set how long the PCS waits for it, the consumer heartbeat time (object 0x1016), a little longer than the BMS's heartbeat period (0x1017). Then a silent BMS stops the PCS.
Put a 120 Ω resistor at each end of the bus, and nowhere else. With none, or with one too many, frames break as the cable gets longer.

anatomy.cobid: An identifier (COB-ID): a function code and a node ID

timing.title: What the bus carries in two seconds
timing.note: TPDO1 goes out every 100 ms (its event timer), the heartbeat every 1000 ms. An emergency message goes out once, when the fault appears, and once more when it clears. The CAN controller chip adds the start bit, the CRC, the acknowledge slot and the stuffing bits (extra bits that keep receivers in step) to every frame. The bytes shown here are what software sees.

playground.file: Try it: the EDS (electronic data sheet) of this lesson's BMS, node 5. It lists the node's objects, so tools know them all before they ask.
playground.device: Who made it and what it is, as a configuration tool shows it.
playground.baud: The bit rates it supports: 500 kbit/s, the bus of this lesson.
playground.heartbeat: Object 0x1017: how often it sends its heartbeat, in ms. Every 1000 ms: the 0x705 frames of this lesson.
playground.types: DataType 0x0006 is UNSIGNED16, 0x0007 is UNSIGNED32: the size of the object's value.
playground.serial: Object 0x1018 sub 4: the serial number the EMS reads with this lesson's SDO.
playground.cobid: TPDO1's identifier: the node number plus 0x180, so 0x185 for node 5.
playground.mapping: What TPDO1 carries first: object 0x2001 sub 1, 0x10 = 16 bits long, the pack voltage.
playground.voltage: The maker's own object for the pack voltage (0x2000 to 0x5FFF is the maker's range): readable, and allowed in a PDO.
playground.encoder: CANopen sends numbers least significant byte first. 8124 is this lesson's pack voltage in 0.1 V: BC 1F, as in its TPDO1.
